topic.name: Computing the Singular Values of a Matrix

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. Any $3\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.
  2. Any $8\times6$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.
  3. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $3 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

  • Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $8 \times 6$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $6 \times 6$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 6} \times {\large 8}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 8} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 6}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 6} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 6}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

  • Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ has two negative singular values.
  2. Any $4\times5$ matrix $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.
  3. Any $8\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have any negative singular value.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $4 \times 5$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $5 \times 5$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 5} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 5}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 5} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 5}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

  • Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $8 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 8$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 8}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 8} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix

question.text: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 0&-2&-1\\1&-2&0 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 0&-2&-1\\1&-2&0 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 0&-2&-1\\1&-2&0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & \!\!-2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0&-2&-1\\1&-2&0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A^T \! A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (1-\lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 8-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} + 2\begin{vmatrix} -2& 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (1 - \lambda)\left[(8 - \lambda)(1 - \lambda) - 4) \right]+2(-2)(1-\lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] (1 - \lambda)(\lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 4)+(-4)(1-\lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] (1 - \lambda)(\lambda^2 - 9 \lambda + 4-4)&= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda (1 - \lambda)(\lambda - 9) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 9, \, 1, \: 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

\begin{align*} \sigma_1 &= \sqrt{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \\[3pt] \sigma_2 &= \sqrt{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 \\[3pt] \sigma_3 &= \sqrt{\lambda_3} = \sqrt{0} = 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix

question.text: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 1&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A^T \! A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (1-\lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (1 - \lambda)((1-\lambda)^2 - 1)&= 0 \\[5pt] (1 - \lambda)(1-2\lambda +\lambda^2- 1)&= 0 \\[5pt] - \lambda ( \lambda-1)(\lambda - 2) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 2, \, 1, \: 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

\begin{align*} \sigma_1 &= \sqrt{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{2} \\[3pt] \sigma_2 &= \sqrt{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 \\[3pt] \sigma_3 &= \sqrt{\lambda_3} = \sqrt{0} = 0 \end{align*}

A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
